pll1d8c8-d1e3477.summary: States that the simplicity and purity of the divine essence is such that there is nothing in it that is not itself; haver and had are the same.
claims: There is nothing in the divine essence that is not the essence.
In God the haver and what is had are the same.

pll1d8c8-d1e3480.summary: Cites Hilary, De Trinitate VII: God who is life, power, light, and spirit is not composed of disparate or weaker elements; all that is in him is one.
claims: God is not composed of parts.
All that is in God is one.

pll1d8c8-d1e3498.summary: Cites the De Trinitate VIII text: God is not composite in the human way, with one thing had and another the haver; he is wholly life, a perfect and infinite nature, not made of disparate parts.
claims: In God the haver and what is had are not distinct.
God is wholly life, a perfect and infinite nature.

pll1d8c8-d1e3516.summary: Cites Boethius, De Trinitate: what is truly one has no number and nothing in it besides what it is, and it cannot become a subject.
claims: The truly one has no number.
There is nothing in God besides what he is.
God cannot be a subject of accidents.

pll1d8c8-d1e3534.summary: Cites the De fide ad Petrum: in God's substance nothing is other than substance, as though one thing were substance and another accidental to it; whatever can be understood there is substance. This is easily said and believed but seen only by a pure heart.
claims: In God nothing is accidental to substance.
Whatever is understood in God is his substance.
Divine simplicity is seen only by the pure in heart.

pll1d8c8-d1e3551.summary: Cites De Trinitate XV: in the nature of each of the three, the one who has is what he has, as an unchangeable and simple substance.
claims: Each divine person is what he has.

pll1d8c8-d1e3568.summary: Cites Isidore: God is called simple either because he does not lose what he has or because he is not other than what is in him. Notes that despite this simplicity there is a Trinity of persons in the divine nature.
claims: God is simple because he does not lose what he has and is not other than what is in him.
There is a Trinity of persons in the simple divine nature.

pll1d8c8-d1e3583.summary: With De civitate Dei XI, explains how simplicity fits the Trinity. It is not that there is only a trinity of names without subsisting persons, as the Sabellians thought; the nature is simple because it is what it has, except for what each person is said relatively to another. The Father has the Son but is not the Son; what is said of God absolutely, such as life, he is. In other things, the haver differs from what is had.
claims: Divine simplicity does not mean a mere trinity of names.
The divine nature is what it has, except for the relative predications between persons.
The Father has the Son but is not the Son.
What God has absolutely, such as life, he is.
In creatures the haver differs from what is had.

pll1d8c8-d1e3601.summary: Concludes the discussion of the divine substance: its identity, unity, immutability, simplicity, and purity have been set out as far as human weakness allows.
claims: The identity, unity, immutability, simplicity, and purity of God have been shown as far as human weakness allows.

pl-l1d8c8.summary: Draws out the purity of divine simplicity: in God's essence there is nothing that is not itself; the haver and what is had are the same. This is supported by Hilary (God is not composed, but all that is in him is one), Boethius (truly one, with no number, nothing besides what it is, and unable to be a subject), the De fide ad Petrum (whatever is understood in God is substance), Augustine (each of the three is what he has), and Isidore. Yet in this simple nature there is a Trinity of persons. With De civitate Dei XI, the nature is called simple not in a Sabellian sense of mere names, but because it is what it has, except for what each person is said relatively to another. Lombard sums up God's identity, unity, immutability, simplicity, and purity as far as our weakness allows.
claims: In the divine essence there is nothing that is not the essence itself.
In God the haver and what is had are identical.
God is not composed of parts or disparate elements.
Nothing in God is accidental; whatever is in him is substance.
Divine simplicity is compatible with a Trinity of persons.
The divine nature is simple because it is what it has, except for the relations by which persons are said to one another.
The Trinity is not a mere trinity of names, as the Sabellians held.
